T. Rowe Price and Franklin Templeton anchor a $210,000 split across three asset managers that pays about $7,943 yearly in dividends.

Invesco's QQQ became an open-end ETF in December 2025, letting the firm collect management fees on it for the first time.

CEO Rob Sharps says, "We do expect pressure on active equities and mutual funds to persist," as T. Rowe clients pulled $28 billion.

Read More: Learn 7 ways to generate income with a $1,000,000+ portfolio (sponsor)

Look at the fund lineup in a typical 401(k), and the same names keep showing up: T. Rowe Price (NASDAQ:TROW), Franklin Templeton (NYSE:BEN), Invesco (NYSE:IVZ). Each is an asset manager, a company that runs mutual funds and ETFs for savers and charges a small yearly fee on the money it looks after. That pool of money is called assets under management, or AUM. The firms that run so much retirement money also trade publicly, and all three pay quarterly dividends.

24/7 Wall St.

The math below shows the annual income from a $70,000 position in each of these three money managers. Across the group, $210,000 would generate $7,943 a year in dividends, using forward yields and prices from the Nov. 9, 2026 close.

Because fees are charged as a percentage of assets, profits rise with markets and with new money coming in. They fall when markets drop, or clients pull cash out. A downturn hits these firms twice: asset values shrink, and the fees on those assets shrink with them. The longer-term pressure comes from savers moving out of actively managed funds and into cheaper index funds and ETFs. At T. Rowe Price, the effective fee rate excluding performance fees slipped to 37.8 basis points from 39.1 a year earlier (a basis point is one-hundredth of a percentage point).

Hedge Funds Dumped Tech at a Near-Record Pace Right Before Chip Stocks Jumped 7%

SOXX
SMH
QQQ
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Quick Read

SOXX jumped 7% and SMH 5% as hedge funds covered shorts after dumping tech at a near-record pace.

Gross leverage plunged far more than net leverage, the biggest drop since March 2020, signaling forced risk-cutting instead of a lasting retreat from chips.

JPMorgan's Dubravko Lakos-Bujas called the pullback largely a "deleveraging event" and kept his 8,000 S&P 500 target.

Read More: Learn 7 ways to generate income with a $1,000,000+ portfolio (sponsor)

Goldman Sachs prime brokerage data through November 6, 2026, showed hedge funds sold technology stocks at a pace roughly matching the highest levels on record since 2016. The morning that data was reported, November 9, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rose 6.9%, its best day since July 30.

24/7 Wall St.

The iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXX) closed at $146.76, up $10.23, or 7.49%, and then slipped to $146.41 after hours. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SMH) gained $23.45, or 5.05%, to $487.41. The Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) rose 3.54% to $679.35.

For chip fund holders, the central question is how much of this move reflected forced selling and how much reflected a review of AI demand. The expansion thesis still depends on the companies providing power, cooling, and networking to the data centers, which we profiled in a free report on seven AI infrastructure names that are not chipmakers.

What the Prime Brokerage Data Actually Shows

Tech was the most heavily net-sold sector, both globally and in the U.S. That selling produced the biggest wave of single-stock net selling in four months. Funds also sold U.S. industrials at the fastest pace since April 2020.

Among U.S. fundamental long/short funds, gross leverage fell 8.7 percentage points to 207.5%, the largest drop since March 2020. Gross leverage is a fund's total long plus short positions measured against its capital, so a drop this size means funds cut both sides at once.

Inflation Puts Rate Relief at Risk

This CPI miss matters because the Fed has been tightening. The upper bound of the fed funds target moved to 4.00% from 3.75% in mid-September. A hot inflation reading makes rate relief less likely.

The bond market had been offering some help. The 10-year Treasury yield was 4.86% Friday, down from 5.21% on October 13. If the CPI report pushes yields back up, growth stocks feel it first.

Tech Gives Back Part of Monday's Rally

On Monday, the Dow surged, and the Nasdaq climbed as tech rebounded from last week's turbulence. This morning, the Dow proxy is higher while the Nasdaq-100 is lower. That split points to money moving out of rate-sensitive growth stocks and into blue chips.

QQQ jumped 4% even as Nvidia sank 4%, because 86 of 101 Nasdaq-100 members rose and Nvidia's drag was only about 0.3 points.

Monolithic Power surged 17% and Applied Materials climbed 11% as chip stocks rebounded, with Nvidia the only semiconductor index member to fall.

Nvidia's board opened an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang, yet the only formal record is his employee memo, with no filing or timeline.

Building a portfolio and living off one are two completely different skills, and almost nobody teaches the second. This problem is what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps, and it is free today. Read more here. (Sponsor)

The Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) closed at $679.35 on November 9, 2026, up 3.54%. That was its best session since May 12, 2025. The Nasdaq-100, the index the fund tracks, rose 917.64 points, or 3.40%, to 27,907.63 from 26,989.99. It was the index's best day since a 3.43% gain on March 31, 2026.

24/7 Wall St.

NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) fell on the same day. It lost 4.27%, or $7.97, to $178.67, the worst result among all 101 index members and its lowest close since April 7.

QQQ owners care about that split because Nvidia has about a 7.1% index weight, second only to Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) at about 8.5%. A rough estimate that multiplies Nvidia's weight by its move puts its drag at about 0.3 percentage points. The index still made a strong gain because 86 members rose and only 15 fell.

NVDA Price Target — 24/7 Wall St.
Chip Stocks Carried the Index Without Its Biggest Chipmaker

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rose 6.85% to 10,033.93 after losing more than 12% in the week ended November 6. Nvidia was the only stock in that index to fall. Monolithic Power Systems (NASDAQ:MPWR) gained 16.6%, and Applied Materials (NASDAQ:AMAT) rose 11.37%, while Apple added 2.43%.
